title: Incident-to-SLO Feedback Playbook: Continuous Improvement Loop
author: Ethan Chen
content:
Summary

This playbook describes a repeatable, auditable process that converts incident findings into concrete SLO / error budget / capacity changes and reliability initiatives. The goal is to close the loop between Post-Incident Reviews (PIRs) and operational policy so that recurring causes drive measurable SLO adjustments, capacity commitments, or tooling investments rather than informal tribal knowledge.

Why this matters

- Prevents repeated outages caused by unclosed SLO gaps.
- Keeps capacity planning honest: incidents should create provable demand signals.
- Reduces subjective escalation: changes follow objective evidence gates.

Scope

- Applies to all customer-facing model serving tiers (hosted API, Dedicated), and control-plane services that affect latency/availability.
- Does not replace emergency mitigation runbooks; it is a follow-up process executed as part of the PIR within 7 calendar days.

Definitions

- Incident: Any event that triggered an oncall escalation, SLO burn > 2x baseline per hour, or customer-impacting degradation.
- SLO Change: A proposal to modify target, window, or SLA mapping for a service.
- Error Budget Action: Any throttle, allocation, or temporary relaxation tied to an error budget.
- Reliability Initiative (RI): A project to reduce recurrence (software fix, automation, capacity add, or tooling).

When to invoke this playbook

1. PIR completes and root cause analysis (RCA) identifies one or more systemic causes.
2. The postmortem has evidence of repeated failure modes or SLO burn that could recur without changes.
3. The incident resulted in customer-visible SLA impact or consumed >= 5% of monthly error budget for the service.

Signals and evidence required to justify changes

- Telemetry: graphs of SLO burn, request latency P50/P95/P99, error-rate per route, and token consumption normalized by model and prompt-length.
- Capacity telemetry: GPU utilization percent, queue lengths, Pod CPU/memory OOMs, autoscaler events, and request throttling logs.
- Release/Deployment context: commit IDs, canary rollout traces, config changes.
- Customer impact evidence: support ticket IDs, affected tenant IDs, and timestamps.

Required artifacts (attach to PIR)

1. SLO impact extract (CSV): timestamp, route, latency bucket, error flag, tenant-id.
2. Capacity snapshot (JSON/YAML): cluster utilization and top-10 queues at incident time.
3. Reproduction summary: minimal reproduction steps or synthetic replay script snippet.

Decision matrix: When to adjust SLO vs. when to take alternate actions

| Condition | Recommended action |
|---|---|
| Single transient spike with identifiable rollout cause and no repeated occurrences | Root-cause fix + monitoring alert; do not change SLO. |
| Repeated burn across 3+ incidents in 30 days or 10%+ monthly error budget consumed | Propose SLO re-evaluation and capacity plan. |
| SLO unattainable given current model/quantization performance | Scope Reliability Initiative (model variant, quantization profile) and update SLO if needed. |
| Clear tenant-specific overload pattern | Tenant throttling policy, capacity partition, and emergency priority-eviction plan. |

Procedure: From PIR to SLO change request (step-by-step)

1. PIR owner tags the incident with the "slo-review" label in the postmortem within 48 hours.
2. Evidence collection: SRE engineer compiles the required artifacts and attaches them to the PIR.
3. Triage meeting (within 5 business days): SRE, Product owner, Platform lead, and the incident responder review artifacts.
4. Outcome options recorded in the meeting notes: 
   - No change (fix + monitoring)
   - Reliability Initiative (project) opened with estimated MTTD/MTTR impact
   - SLO Change Request (see template below)
   - Capacity Allocation / Reserved Commitment request
5. If SLO Change Request selected, follow the SLO change checklist and open an SLO PR.
6. Implementation, monitoring, and verification: run a 14-day shadow comparison after change before closing the loop.

SLO Change Checklist (must be satisfied to approve change)

- Evidence: time-series demonstrating the issue measured against existing SLO window.
- Customer impact summary and business rationale.
- Alternatives considered (capacity add, throttling, cache, model variant).
- Quantified expected impact on error budget (simulated).
- Rollback plan and metric guardrails with precise thresholds.
- Reviewers assigned (SRE lead, Product, Platform).

SLO Change Request template (fill when opening PR)

- service: <service-name>
- current_slo: "99.9% availability, 1m window"
- proposed_slo: "99.8% availability, 5m window"
- justification: short summary of evidence and business impact
- simulations: link to synthetic replay results (CSV)
- verification-plan: metric checks and dashboards to monitor post-change
- rollback-condition: e.g., "If 24h rolling error budget consumption > 15% or P99 latency regression > 20%"

Example SLO change PR body (text to paste into GitHub/Confluence)

"This PR proposes lowering the availability SLO from 99.9% to 99.8% for /v1/generate when serving large-context Llama-extended models. Evidence: three incidents in 21 days where the P99 latency exceeded the configured autoscaler warmup window causing 6m+ tail-latency spikes; simulated fix would reduce monthly error budget burn from 18% to 9%. Proposal includes a verification window of 14 days with automated rollback if error budget burn increases > 10% relative to baseline."

Capacity planning tie-ins

- If incident source is capacity-related (GPU saturation, long queue latencies), submit a capacity request ticket with: peak delta, targeted region, node type, estimated monthly cost, and urgency tier.
- Default SRE capacity response target: triage within 3 business days; capacity procurement within 14 business days for tier-2/routine requests.
- Emergency capacity: immediate request via the oncall slack channel and PagerDuty escalation; include cluster snapshots and tenant impact.

Operational tooling checklist (queries and dashboards to include with PIR)

- SLO burn dashboard: per-route, per-tenant burn and rolling-window breakdown.
- Top-k latency contributors: traces grouped by model, prompt-length, and GPU queue.
- Autoscaler event histogram: scale-up/down latency and missed-scale events.
- Token cost vs. latency scatter: identify economic vs. latency trade-offs.

Example Grafana/Loki queries (text)

- P95 latency for service X: rate(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"service-x\"}[5m])) by (le)))
- Error budget burn rate: increase(rate(error_count_total{service=\"svc\"}[1m]) / rate(request_count_total{service=\"svc\"}[1m]))

Runbook snippet: Tenant emergency throttling (manual sequence)

1. Identify tenant ID(s) consuming top tokens via dashboard.
2. Create temporary tenant policy: 
   - kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
   apiVersion: rbac.platform/v1
   kind: TenantThrottle
   metadata:
     name: emergency-throttle-<tenant-id>
   spec:
     tenantId: <tenant-id>
     maxQPS: 10
     maxTokensPerMin: 10000
   EOF
3. Notify customer-success and record change in incident timeline.
4. Monitor token & queue metrics for 30 minutes, then iterate.

Verification and closing the loop

- The PIR owner must add a follow-up checkpoint to the incident page at 7 and 21 days describing observed metrics vs expected.
- For SLO changes, require a 14-day shadow verification where old and new SLOs are measured in parallel (shadowing requests or synthetic traffic).
- If metrics diverge from the expected, follow the rollback conditions defined in the SLO PR.

Reliability initiatives and tracking

- Create an RI ticket for medium/large work items; include expected MTTD/MTTR improvement and estimated effort (story points or engineering days).
- Tag RIs with the incident ID and SLO change PR for traceability.

Incident review standards (what reviewers must check)

- Evidence completeness: required artifacts present and timestamped.
- Reproducibility: reproduction steps or synthetic replay available.
- Cost/benefit: capacity and SLO changes include a cost estimate.
- Ownership: assignee and code owner identified for each action.

Reporting and governance

- Monthly SLO review board (SRE lead, Platform, Product) will audit all SLO Changes approved in the previous 30 days and validate verification windows.
- Quarterly reliability metric report will summarize: incidents, number of SLO changes approved, error budget variance, and RIs opened/completed.

Appendix A: Example evidence checklist (copy into PIR)

- [ ] Time-series exports for SLO windows (CSV)
- [ ] Capacity snapshot (JSON)
- [ ] List of affected tenants (anonymized if required)
- [ ] Synthetic replay results (CSV + description)
- [ ] Proposed SLO PR link or RI ticket link

Appendix B: Quickplay commands (for SRE oncall)

- Export recent top-100 slow traces: curl -G \"https://tracing.internal/api/search?service=service-x&limit=100&min_duration_ms=500\" -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TRACING_TOKEN\" > slow-traces.json
- Capture autoscaler events: kubectl -n platform logs deploy/autoscaler --since=1h | grep "scale" > autoscaler-events.log

Notes and references

- Related: SRE capacity onboarding and SLO admission playbook.
- Contact: SRE lead (sre-leads@redwood.com) for disputes on SLO changes.
